name: Balanced Binary Search Trees
description: Recall that a binary search tree is a rooted binary tree, whose nodes each store a key and each have at most two distinguished subtrees, left and right. The key in each node must be greater than any key stored in the left subtree, and less than any key stored in the right subtree. The depth of a vertex is the number of edges on the simple path from the vertex to the root. In particular, the depth of the root is $$$0$$$. Let's call a binary search tree perfectly balanced if there doesn't exist a binary search tree with the same number of vertices that has a strictly smaller sum of depths of its vertices. Let's call a binary search tree with integer keys striped if both of the following conditions are satisfied for every vertex $$$v$$$: If $$$v$$$ has a left subtree whose root is $$$u$$$, then the parity of the key of $$$v$$$ is different from the parity of the key of $$$u$$$. If $$$v$$$ has a right subtree whose root is $$$w$$$, then the parity of the key of $$$v$$$ is the same as the parity of the key of $$$w$$$. You are given a single integer $$$n$$$. Find the number of perfectly balanced striped binary search trees with $$$n$$$ vertices that have distinct integer keys between $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$, inclusive. Output this number modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
input_specification: The only line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^6$$$), denoting the required number of vertices.
output_specification: Output the number of perfectly balanced striped binary search trees with $$$n$$$ vertices and distinct integer keys between $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$, inclusive, modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1237E — Balanced Binary Search Trees [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
